/-!
# Erdős Problem 1106

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/1064](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1106)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Nat Finset Filter Topology

namespace Erdos1106

/-- The partition function p(n) is the number of ways to write n as a sum of positive
integers (where the order of the summands does not matter). -/
def p : ℕ → ℕ := fun n => Fintype.card (Nat.Partition n)

/--
Let $p(n)$ be the partition number of $n$ and $F(n)$ be the number of distinct prime factors of
$∏_{i= 1} ^ {n} p(n)$, then $F(n)$ tends to infinity when $n$ tends to infinity.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1106.parts.i :
    answer(sorry) ↔ Tendsto (fun n => #(∏ i ∈ Icc 1 n, p i).primeFactors) atTop atTop := by
  sorry

/--
Let $p(n)$ be the partition number of $n$ and $F(n)$ be the number of distinct prime factors of
$∏_{i= 1} ^ {n} p(n)$, $F(n)>n$ for sufficiently large $n$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1106.parts.ii :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ᶠ n in atTop, #(∏ i ∈ Icc 1 n, p i).primeFactors > n := by
  sorry

end Erdos1106

findings.description: The docstring defines F(n) using ∏_{i=1}^n p(n), which is p(n)^n, rather than the cumulative product ∏_{i=1}^n p(i). The Lean statement correctly uses `p i`. These products count different distinct prime factors: at n = 3 the docstring's product has one distinct prime factor, while the intended product has two; both counts were verified in Lean.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1106 defines F(n) as the number of distinct prime factors of ∏_{1≤k≤n} p(k), and asks whether F(n) tends to infinity.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace `p(n)` by `p(i)` inside the docstring's product. Leave the theorem's right-hand side unchanged.

findings.description: The docstring repeats the same incorrect product ∏_{i=1}^n p(n), whereas the source and the Lean statement use the cumulative product ∏_{i=1}^n p(i). This is a prose error only; the formal eventual inequality is faithful.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1106 defines F(n) using ∏_{1≤k≤n} p(k) and asks: “Is F(n)>n for all sufficiently large n?”
findings.suggested_fix: Replace `p(n)` by `p(i)` inside the docstring's product. No change to the Lean statement is needed.

status_issues.source_status: Solved affirmatively. The source attributes F(n)→∞ to Schinzel's observation in the Oberwolfach problem book, with details in Erdős–Ivić [ErIv90], page 69. It also records the stronger lower bound F(n) ≫ log n proved by Schinzel–Wirsing [ScWi87]. The eventual inequality in part (ii) remains open.
status_issues.evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/1106: “Schinzel noted in the Oberwolfach problem book that F(n)→∞ follows from the asymptotic formula for p(n) and a result of Tijdeman [Ti73]”; the next paragraph records F(n) ≫ log n.
status_issues.suggested_change: Change part (i) to `@[category research solved, AMS 11]`, replace its answer slot with `answer(True)`, and document the historical result. Retain the existing mathematical right-hand side and leave part (ii) open.

review.notes: No substantive mathematical misformalization was found in the definition or either theorem. In /workspace/review/scratch.lean, successful checks evaluated p(0) through p(10), proved positivity of every partition number and cumulative product, checked the empty-product cases, established the exact prime-divisor membership condition, and proved the explicit quantifier equivalents of both filter statements. Thus the default `primeFactors 0 = ∅` is unreachable here, and allowing n = 0 does not affect either asymptotic claim. The final scratch compilation succeeded without warnings or errors. Direct source requests were challenged; the main page was read through the HTML reader mirror.
